title: The Word Before the Word
teaser: Euangelion did not begin in Greek. The Hebrew prophets had been waiting on the same news, in their own language, for centuries.
theme: The gospel was already a word before it was an announcement. Isaiah's runners and watchmen are waiting for the same news Mark begins announcing.
framework: Chiastic build — the Hebrew root of the Greek word, and the centuries-long waiting underneath it.

modules.passage: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

modules.heading: The Watchman on the Wall
modules.body:
There is a picture buried in this sentence, and the King James English keeps it from being smoothed away. A man is running. He is coming up the side of a mountain on a footpath. Below the wall of a city, a watchman has been on duty for days, scanning the horizon for the one figure he has been told to look for. The watchman sees feet first — feet against the skyline, feet on the ridge, feet that mean the runner has come close enough to read.

That is what the prophet sees. "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings."

It is a strange line to call beautiful. Feet are not beautiful. Feet are dusty, calloused, often ugly, and after a long run probably bleeding. The Hebrew is not flinching from any of that. The beauty is not in the feet. The beauty is in what the feet mean. The runner has arrived. The waiting is ending. The watchman can step down off the wall.

If you came in on Day 1, you met a Greek word — euangelion — that Mark borrowed from the public squares of the Roman empire. Today we are going further back. The word Mark borrowed had a Hebrew shadow that ran centuries before it. The runner Mark hears coming over the gospel's first horizon was already running, in another language, in a much older book.

This matters even if you are coming to all of this with suspicion. The Old Testament — the part of the Bible with the long lists and the war stories and the famously hard-to-warm-up-to portrayals of God — is not a separate religion that Christianity outgrew. It is the soil the New Testament is planted in. The single Greek word the New Testament keeps reaching for is, underneath, a Hebrew concept, and that concept lives in some of the most quiet and exhausted passages in all of scripture.

You do not need to take that on faith. Today we will read one verse from Isaiah and one verse from Paul's letter to the Romans, side by side, and let them argue for themselves.

Today's question is small and patient: where did this word come from before the word existed?

modules.definition: Tidings, news; specifically, the report a runner brings from a battlefield or a court.
modules.rootMeaning: From the verb basar (בָּשַׂר, H1319), meaning "to bear tidings, to announce." Besorah is the noun the verb produces — the news itself.
modules.usage: In the Hebrew Bible, besorah is used for both good news and bad news, depending on the runner. In 2 Samuel 18, two messengers race down a hillside with news of Absalom's death; the king watches them come and asks, "Is the young man safe?" In 2 Kings 7, four lepers stumble onto an abandoned enemy camp and say to one another, "This is a day of besorah." The word does not, on its own, name salvation. It names a runner with information that changes what the city does next.
modules.usageNote: Around 250 BC, Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek — the version called the Septuagint. When they came to the cognate verb basar in Isaiah 52:7 and 40:9 and 61:1, they reached for forms of euangelion and euangelizomai. The Greek word the New Testament uses was, in the bilingual Jewish world Jesus walked into, already carrying the freight of the Hebrew prophets. By the time Mark writes "the beginning of the euangelion of Jesus Christ," the word is not new. It is a word that has been waiting.

relatedWords.note: the underlying verb (H1319), "to bear tidings" — the action the runner is performing
the participle form, "the one who bears tidings" — the runner himself, the figure on the mountain in Isaiah 52:7

modules.heading: Inside the Book of Comfort
modules.body:
To hear Isaiah 52:7 the way its first hearers heard it, you have to know what year it is and where the people are.

The book we now call Isaiah is a long, layered prophetic work. The historical core dates to the eighth century BC, but chapters 40 through 55 — the section scholars often call the Book of Comfort — speak into a much later moment. The setting is the Babylonian exile. In 587 BC, the Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar broke through the walls of Jerusalem, burned the temple, and dragged the surviving leadership of the southern kingdom of Judah east in chains. The exiles lived in and around Babylon for roughly seventy years.

This was not just a political defeat. It was a theological catastrophe. The covenant God had made with Abraham involved a particular land, a city, and a sanctuary. All three had been taken. The temple, the building where the people had been told the presence of God dwelt, had been pulled down stone from stone. The God of Israel had, by every available reading, lost. The gods of Babylon had won.

Into that long humiliation, the second half of Isaiah speaks.

The Book of Comfort opens with one of the most famous lines in the Hebrew Bible: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." The voice that follows is not triumphant. It is tender. It is addressed to a community of trauma survivors who have been told for two generations that their God could not protect them. The prophet's job is to convince them that the silence is ending.

The shape of the announcement, chapter after chapter, is the same. A messenger is coming. Watch the horizon. In 40:9: "O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain." In 61:1: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek." That last line is the one Jesus will later read aloud in his hometown synagogue, in Luke 4, and then sit down and say, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."

In the middle of all this, Isaiah 52:7 stands as the most concentrated image of the announcement.

The verse pictures a returning king. In the ancient near east, when a king came back to his city after a campaign, a runner went ahead of him. The runner's job was to climb the last ridge before the city came in view, plant himself on the highest visible piece of ground, and shout the news down to the watchmen on the wall: he is coming, and he is coming as victor. The campaign is over. The captives are coming home. Open the gates.

The runner in 52:7 is not a generic positive message. He is a herald with a specific announcement. His four shouted lines are: good tidings, peace, good tidings of good, salvation. And the substance is at the end: "Thy God reigneth." Your God, the one you thought had been defeated by Babylon, has come back, and not as a refugee but as a king.

The exiles were not waiting for an upgrade in their circumstances. They were waiting for someone they had been told was real to actually arrive. Anyone who has waited on something to keep its word — a person, a system, a faith they were given as children — knows the shape of that waiting. The Babylonians are different. The waiting is the same.

Mark, when he opens his short gospel with euangelion, knows exactly which mountain he is putting his runner on.

modules.ancientTruth: In Isaiah 52:7, a runner climbs the last ridge above a defeated city and shouts that the king is coming home as victor. The exiles are about to hear that the silence is ending.
modules.modernApplication: Six centuries later, Paul writes to a small house church in Rome about how the news of Jesus reaches a person. He reaches back into the Book of Comfort and lifts Isaiah 52:7 directly off the page.
modules.connection: Paul is making a structural claim. The runner Isaiah saw on the mountain and the preacher knocking on a Roman door are the same figure, separated by centuries but carrying the same message. The captivity Isaiah's runner ended is the same shape as the captivity Paul's gospel is announcing the end of. The exile is wider than Babylon.
modules.question: If the same image is doing the same work in both writers — Isaiah in the eighth century BC and Paul in the first century AD — what does that say about the news itself?
modules.answer: The news is older than the announcement of it. There has been a runner on the horizon as long as there have been people who knew, somewhere in their bones, that the way things are is not the way things are supposed to be. Isaiah names the watchmen. Paul names the messengers. Same horizon. Same feet.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Read Paul's quotation of Isaiah 52:7 in Romans 10 as if you are the watchman.

emphasis: How can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?
How can they preach unless they are sent?
How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
modules.passage: How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!'

modules.heading: Knowing God, Knowing Ourselves
modules.body:
Read Paul's chain of questions slowly. They run backward, like a person tracing a string to its source. How can a person call on someone they do not believe in? How can they believe in someone they have not heard about? How can they hear if no one preaches? How can preaching happen if no one is sent? Each question peels off another assumption until what is left is a sender. Someone has to put the runner on the road.

Then Paul does something startling. He cites Isaiah 52:7 as if the prophet were finishing his sentence for him. "As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.'" Paul is reading his present moment through the eyes of a prophet six centuries dead. The runner Isaiah saw is the runner Paul is sending now.

This is the day's deepest claim. The Christian gospel is not a different message from the Hebrew gospel. It is the Hebrew gospel arrived. The God who did not show up to the exiles in Babylon as quickly as they wanted Him to is the God who, six centuries later, walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem. Same God. Same promise. Different chapter of the same story.

If you have been told the Old Testament God and the New Testament God are two different gods, that's a teaching the church rejected as heresy in the second century — over a long argument with a man named Marcion. There is one God, telling one long story.

A reader coming into this with religious fatigue or prior church damage needs that named, because it is one of the most common reasons people lose patience with the Bible halfway through. If the angry-God-of-the-Old-Testament passages have been used as a club against you, please hear this carefully. You were not wrong to find some of those passages alarming. You may have been wrong about whose voice was alarming you and to what end. The Book of Comfort is in the Old Testament. The watchman on the wall is in the Old Testament. The runner with beautiful feet is in the Old Testament. He has been signaling for centuries that the signal is good news.

This is where John Calvin can help, even if his name carries baggage. Calvin opens his enormous theological work, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, with a sentence that has anchored Western Christian thinking for almost five hundred years:

"Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves."

What Calvin is doing in that one sentence is what the Book of Comfort does across sixteen chapters. You cannot understand who you are without understanding who God is, and you cannot understand who God is without coming to terms with who you actually are. The two knowledges are inseparable.

The waiting in Isaiah is the same shape as the waiting in the modern reader. That is the line. The exiles in Babylon were not first wrong about politics. They were wrong, partly, about themselves. They had assumed they understood their situation — beaten by a stronger empire — when what they had been carrying was a much older problem with the human heart that the political defeat had only exposed. The good news Isaiah's runner carries is not just "the king is coming home." It is "and you will recognize him because you will at the same moment recognize yourselves."

Good news is recognized only by people who know they need news. A person convinced they are doing fine has no use for a herald. The exiles, by virtue of the wreckage around them, knew they were in trouble. The reader of this paragraph, depending on what kind of week it has been, may also know.

What Isaiah and Paul are doing together — and what Calvin spent forty years writing about — is putting these two recognitions back together. The runner shouts good tidings, and the watchman recognizes both the runner and himself in the same moment. That is what good news does. It gives you back a clearer view of the world and a clearer view of yourself at once, and it does this with the speed only news can have. It is not analysis. It is announcement.

Tomorrow we get to the announcement itself. Today we are still on the mountain, watching the feet appear on the ridge.

modules.title: What Are You Waiting to Hear?
modules.prompt:
Set the reading aside for a few minutes. If you have somewhere to write — a notebook, a phone note, a scrap of paper — open it. Writing is better than thinking, because the hand slows the mind down enough for the truer answer to come up.

The question is small and direct: what good news are you waiting to hear?

Not abstractly. Specifically. If a runner came over the ridge and reached your gate today, what would the news have to be for you to recognize it as the news you have been listening for? Write a sentence, a list, the name of one person, one decision that has been pending too long.

Let yourself surprise yourself. Many of us have a respectable answer ready — the one we would give a counselor in five minutes. Sit past that one. The truer answer is usually a layer down.

When you have written something, sit with it for a breath. The runner of Isaiah 52:7 was not running toward a community that had named the news clearly first. He was running because the news was true whether or not the city had figured out how to ask for it.
modules.follow_up: If nothing comes up, that is also data. Some of us have been so long without permission to want anything that we cannot find the want. The runner comes over that ridge too.

modules.heading: If You Are One of Isaiah's Exiles
modules.body:
There is a chance, depending on how this week is going, that the geography in Isaiah is closer than it sounds. The exiles in Babylon did not feel exiled because they had been moved a particular distance from a city. They felt exiled because the life they had been promised had not arrived. The temple had been knocked down. The covenant they had been raised inside had visibly failed to protect them. They were living in a place where everything they had been taught to expect had quietly stopped showing up.

A modern reader does not need a Babylonian army to know that feeling.

For some of you, the exile is religious. You were raised inside a faith that ended up wounding you, or asking you to pretend in ways you cannot any longer pretend. You walked out, or were walked out, and the city you came from has not gotten quieter behind you. You can still hear the songs. You just cannot live as if any of it was true the way you were once told it was. That is a kind of exile.

For some of you, it is not religious at all. It is the slow erosion of trust in institutions, in stories, in the shape of the life you were told you would have if you did the right things. The job did not come. The marriage did not stay. The body did not hold up. The list of things you used to be sure of has thinned.

For some of you it is more private. A steady, low-grade ache underneath the day that you have stopped trying to name. That, too, is a watchman on a wall, scanning for a runner.

Isaiah is writing for all three. The Book of Comfort is not religious literature for people who have their lives in order. It is for people whose lives have come apart. The whole reason the prophet speaks tenderly is that the audience cannot bear another sermon.

If that is you, please hear this carefully. You are not outside the reach of this announcement because you are tired of religion. You are inside its target audience. The runner of Isaiah 52:7 was not running to people whose theology was tidy. He was running to people whose theology had been knocked down by the events of their actual lives, and who had reached the point where the next true thing they could say about God would have to be said by someone else.

The job today is not to fix anything. It is not to make a decision. It is much smaller. It is to climb back up onto the wall.

Climbing back up onto the wall means letting yourself believe — at least long enough to read tomorrow — that there might still be a runner on the way. That the silence between the promise and the keeping is not, finally, the whole story. The exiles were not wrong to be in pain. They were just wrong about whether the pain meant the story was over.

The watchman is not producing the news. He is also not denying it. He is doing the small, unglamorous work of looking — keeping his eyes on the place where, if anything is going to come, it will come.

That is enough for today. You do not have to know yet. You just have to look.

modules.prompt: When you wrote down what good news you are waiting to hear, what came up first — and was there a layer underneath that you almost missed?
additionalQuestions: If the runner of Isaiah 52:7 reached your gate today, would you be more relieved or more afraid? What does that say about how long you have been waiting?
Where in your life are you currently a watchman on a wall — scanning the horizon for something that has not yet arrived?
If Calvin is right that knowing God and knowing yourself come together, which one have you been quieter about lately, and why?

modules.heading: The Word Was Already on Its Way
modules.body:
Today's reading was not, finally, about a Hebrew word. It was about a piece of news that has been on its way for a very long time.

When Mark, in the late 60s AD, opened his short account of the life of Jesus with the Greek word euangelion, he was not coining a term. He was reaching for a word the Septuagint translators had already stitched into Isaiah more than two centuries earlier. When those translators chose euangelion to render besorah, they were translating a sound the prophets had been making since the exiles came home. Underneath the Greek of the New Testament is the Hebrew of the prophets. Underneath that is a runner who has been on the road, in the imagination of the people of God, for as long as anyone can remember.

The Bible is not a book that arrived all at once. It grew up in the slow, patient way a hill grows up out of a plain — geological, layered, unhurried. The line you read today in Isaiah and the line you read today in Paul are separated by six centuries and roughly fifteen hundred miles. They are saying the same thing. That is what the people who put the canon together meant for you to notice.

It also means something for how you can come to this. You do not have to start at chapter one. You do not have to know all the names. The runner has been on the road longer than your particular life. He is not surprised that you are arriving in the middle of the story.

Tomorrow the runner reaches the gate, and says, in the most compressed shape the early church ever gave it, what the news actually is. The four-line summary Paul says he received and passed on — written down within five years of the events it describes — is the oldest fixed-form summary the church has ever had. It is the message the runners have been carrying.

For today, you can stay on the wall.

The one thing worth taking away, if only one thing lands: the good news the New Testament announces is not a new word. It is a Hebrew word in Greek clothes. The waiting in the Old Testament is the waiting Christianity says has now ended. The God who feels distant in the Old Testament is the God who, in the New Testament, sends His own feet up the mountain. Same story. Same God. Different chapter.

If you have been one of the watchmen, please keep watching. The feet are on the ridge. The runner is closer than yesterday. The next reading is the runner's mouth opening.

modules.title: A Prayer from the Wall
modules.prayerText:
God of Isaiah and Paul, God of the long delays and the quiet keeping —

I did not know I had been waiting until today. Some of the waiting I named in writing. Some of it is still in places I cannot quite say out loud yet.

If the runner of Isaiah's mountain is the same runner the New Testament describes, I am asking, gently, to stay on the wall a little longer. I do not have a tidy belief to offer You today. I have a horizon I am willing to keep watching.

If You have been speaking through old languages and older voices, please give me ears that can hear what is on its way without forcing me to pretend I have already heard.

I am not promising what I cannot promise. I am only saying, today, that I am still looking.

Amen.

modules.title: On the Wall
modules.commitment: Today I will let the wall be enough. I will not force a conclusion. I will keep my eyes on the horizon and let the runner come.
leavingAtCross: The pressure to have the right religious vocabulary before I can hear the announcement.
The fear that the Old Testament God is a different God than the One the gospels describe.
The rehearsed story about what good news I am supposed to want.
receivingFromCross: The Hebrew word besorah and the picture of the watchman on the wall as a portable image of where I am.
The promise that the runner has been on the road longer than my life and is not surprised to find me here.
modules.content: Today I will let the wall be enough. I will not force a conclusion. I will keep my eyes on the horizon and let the runner come.

modules.title: Sources for Today's Reading
modules.intro: The voice quoted in today's reading, with full citation and brief context. Scripture and lexicon sources are also listed.

resources.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion
resources.author: John Calvin
resources.citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Ford Lewis Battles, ed. John T. McNeill, Library of Christian Classics, vols. XX-XXI (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1960), Book I, Chapter 1, Section 1.
resources.quote: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
resources.context: Calvin's Institutes opens with this sentence. The pairing — knowledge of God and knowledge of self — stayed in place from the first edition in 1536 through the final Latin revision in 1559. Day 2 frames Isaiah's exiles as an audience in whom both knowledges arrive together.

resources.title: Isaiah 52:7 (King James Version)
resources.citation: King James Version, 1611. Public domain. KJV is used for the prophetic cadence — the Hebrew of Isaiah's poetry sings in a way most modern translations flatten.
resources.context: Isaiah 40-55, the Book of Comfort, addresses the Babylonian exile (587 BC and the decades following). The watchman-and-runner image in 52:7 is the most concentrated picture of the announcement that the captivity is over.

resources.title: Romans 10:14-15 (Berean Standard Bible)
resources.citation: Berean Standard Bible (CC0), 2023. Public-domain modern English; chosen for clarity in Pauline argument.
resources.context: Paul, writing around AD 57, quotes Isaiah 52:7 directly. The runner of the Old Testament is the gospel preacher of the New Testament.

resources.title: בְּשׂוֹרָה (besorah) — Hebrew lexicon
resources.citation: Strong's Hebrew H1309; underlying verb basar (בָּשַׂר), Strong's H1319. Reference: Brown-Driver-Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament (Oxford: Clarendon, 1907), public domain.
resources.context: The Septuagint translators (~250 BC) chose forms of euangelion / euangelizomai to render basar / besorah — directly linking the Hebrew prophetic vocabulary to the Greek word the New Testament uses.
